description: We are a passionate and creative team interested in technology, space exploration, and game development, excited to combine our skills to build an innovative and educational NASA-inspired game.
summary:
We built Shackleton Station, a 3D survival game for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in a web browser with no download or account. The player is an astronaut at a small base on the rim of Shackleton Crater, at the Moon's south pole, and must survive four work shifts. Oxygen, food and power keep running down, and every fix has a cost: grow lights make food but drain the battery, and water in the shelter walls blocks radiation but can't become oxygen. Mini-games teach the science behind each system, like splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen or patching a leak after a micrometeoroid hit.
The challenge asked for real engineering trade-offs built on real NASA data. The terrain comes from LRO laser altimeter maps, particle storms replay NASA DONKI records, and drain rates use NASA's life-support baseline values. The in-game Databank credits a source for every fact.
Artemis is sending astronauts to this region. Kids who play learn why a base there is hard to keep alive by making the kinds of choices those crews will face.
details:
What it does and how it works?

Shackleton Station is a 3D survival game for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in a web browser, with no download or account. The player is an astronaut at a small base on the rim of Shackleton Crater, at the Moon's south pole, and has to get through four work shifts of six real minutes each. Oxygen, food and battery power run down the whole time, so the player keeps deciding what to fix first.

Each refill happens in a short mini-game that teaches the science behind it. To make oxygen you split water at the Electrolysis unit, which costs water and power. Grow lights feed potatoes, lettuce and radishes but drain the battery. When a real solar particle storm arrives, you run to the storm shelter, where water in the walls blocks radiation but can no longer become oxygen. A micrometeoroid can crack the solar array or punch a hole in the habitat, and you find and patch it in a repair game. Supplies ordered from Earth wait for the real 1.28-second light delay. On Day 1, a helper robot called Volt walks you through the base and explains each machine out loud.

Benefits:

Kids learn how a Moon base stays alive by running one. Every refill costs something else, so the trade-offs engineers face show up in play instead of being explained in text. The science is simplified by leaving details out, never by saying something false. Every fact in the game has a source, and kids can read the sources in the in-game Databank.

Intended impact:

Artemis is sending astronauts to the lunar south pole. We want a child who finishes the game to know that oxygen there has to be made from water, that power is shared between every machine, and why a crew needs a shelter during a solar storm. Because the game is free and runs in a browser, a classroom can use it on ordinary school computers.

Tools and technology:

We wrote the game in JavaScript, HTML and CSS, using three.js for the 3D world and Vite to build it. Post-processing uses the pmndrs postprocessing and n8ao libraries, and Volt's voice is eSpeak (through meSpeak) running in a Web Worker. The game logic is kept separate from the graphics and covered by 189 unit tests with Node's test runner. A balance simulator has bots play the real rules to check that the mission is hard but possible. We used Git and GitHub, with GitHub Pages for hosting, and Claude Code as a coding assistant. The data comes from NASA BVAD (life support), DONKI and RadLab (space weather and radiation), LRO LOLA (terrain), the Yale Bright Star Catalog through NASA HEASARC, and JPL Horizons. We used no special hardware, and the game targets 60 fps on a mid-range laptop.

What makes it creative?

The world is built from real measurements. The crater rim comes from LRO laser altimeter maps, so the low Sun hides behind real hills. The sky holds 1,640 real stars, and Live mode shows where the Sun and Earth are over the south pole right now. Particle storms replay the May 2024 solar storms. The lessons are arcade games, like zapping water molecules apart. There is no air outside, so footsteps there are a low crunch you feel through your boots instead of hear.

Factors we considered:


- Accuracy: we checked each fact against a source, and numbers chosen for game balance are labeled as such. Archived data says "Replay of real data from (date)", and only live data says "Live".
- Age: text is at least 16 px, contrast is at least 4.5:1, there are no more than four gauges on screen, and real terms come with a one-line explanation.
- Failure: losing doesn't end the game. A player whose gauge hits zero wakes up in the habitat and loses time.
- Performance: a Low/High graphics setting keeps the game playable on school computers.
- Licensing: textures and music are public domain, and Volt's voice is GPL-3.0.
